# flutter_constraint_layout

> A faithful port of Android ConstraintLayout to Flutter, in pure Dart. Every child is a direct child of one `ConstraintLayout`, and each child declares where its edges go (pinned to the parent or to a sibling by id) and how it is sized. The widget tree stays flat instead of nesting rows, columns, and stacks, and the same layout runs on iOS, Android, web, macOS, Windows, and Linux.

flutter_constraint_layout is pure Dart (no native code, no platform setup) and runs on every Flutter platform. Add it with `flutter pub add flutter_constraint_layout` (or `flutter_constraint_layout: ^1.0.0` under `dependencies` in `pubspec.yaml`) and import `package:flutter_constraint_layout/flutter_constraint_layout.dart`, which brings in every widget, dimension, link, and helper. It requires Dart 3.12 or newer and Flutter 3.44 or newer, and its API is designed around Dart dot shorthands. Children are declared with the `Constrained` widget, each keyed by a `Symbol` id, and positioned with dot-shorthand constraints such as `.startOf(parent, margin: 16)`, `.fixed(56)`, `.matchConstraint`, `.percent(0.5)`, `.spread`, `.packed`, and `.gone`. Helpers like `Guideline` and `Barrier`, chains, aspect ratios, circular positioning, and the virtual `ConstraintFlow` and `ConstraintGrid` layouts cover the arrangements that usually require extra wrapper widgets. A `ConstraintGroup(id:, referenced:, visibility:)` sets the visibility of several children at once, like Android's `Group`: its `visibility` replaces that of every child in `referenced`, and, as Android's `Group` is, it is a 0 x 0 widget at the layout's origin that never moves or sizes anything, so nothing can link to it or reference it. Under the hood the package runs Android's own layout pipeline, ported line by line from androidx constraintlayout to pure Dart: each child is measured as Android's view measurer measures a child view, then Android's `Direct` pass places everything that follows directly from the links and its Cassowary solver settles the rest (chains, aspect ratios, percent sizes), in Android's 32-bit float arithmetic, and every child is placed at the integer frame Android computes. The default, `ConstraintLayout(optimizationLevel: OptimizationLevel.standard)`, is Android's default optimization level; the dependency-graph levels (`OptimizationLevel.graph`, `OptimizationLevel.graphWrap`) are an opt-in that runs where Android runs the graph. Checked against Android's own code, it gives Android's frames, with 0 differences, on 60,000 real widget trees and more than 1.8 million engine layouts. Frames are whole logical pixels (there is no device-pixel mode), content such as text is measured by Flutter rather than by Android's `TextView`, and `ConstraintGrid`, which follows the core grid behind Compose, is outside that parity check. A barrier's own `margin` keeps its sign in right-to-left text, as on Android, so a gap that should mirror goes on the links that target the barrier. Link a child's `top` or `bottom` to a barrier, not its `baseline`: when the solver rather than the `Direct` pass places the barrier (at `OptimizationLevel.none` always, and at the default level when the barrier references a widget `Direct` does not place, such as a chain member, a percent size, or, in a layout that sizes its height to its content, a widget linked to the layout's bottom), a baseline linked to the barrier's `top` or `bottom` can make the solver fail, as Android's does; the layout then prints `EXCEPTION : Null check operator used on a null value` (`EXCEPTION : Unexpected null value.` in a web debug build), collapses the children the solve had not yet placed into its top-left corner, a `.wrapContent` one at 0 x 0, and, if it sizes its height to its content, as a list item does, comes out 0 high. On an axis where the layout sizes to its content (inside a scroll view), a `.wrapContent` or `.matchParent` child is measured with unbounded constraints, as Android measures it under an `UNSPECIFIED` spec, so a child that needs a bound there, such as a `ListView`, fails with an error that names it and the axis.

**Read the docs first.** The Markdown file below is the website's docs page in one file (installation, anchoring edges, right-to-left rules, bias and centering, constraint dimensions, aspect ratios, chains, guidelines, barriers, circular positioning, visibility and gone, groups, the virtual Flow and Grid layouts, a worked example, and the engine internals). Fetch it before answering questions about this package: it is compact Markdown written to be read in one pass. It is a guided tour, not the full reference: the package README, listed after it, is the full guide and also covers z-order, sizing inside scroll views and intrinsic sizing, the debug overlay, unknown and duplicate ids, common mistakes, Android parity, optimization levels, performance, and the limitations and differences from Android.

**Build each `Symbol` id the same way everywhere.** A literal id such as `#avatar` is fine when every link and `referenced` entry also uses the literal. For ids made in a loop with `Symbol('item$i')`, refer to them only through the same call, for example a helper `Symbol item(int i) => Symbol('item$i');`, never through a literal such as `#item0` or a `const Symbol('item0')`. Release and profile WebAssembly builds, and builds compiled with `--obfuscate`, rename symbol literals, so there `#item0` is not equal to `Symbol('item0')` and a link that mixes the two forms is silently skipped, even though it works in debug builds.

**Links must not loop back on themselves.** Four kinds of loop leave none of their children a position to start from: two children whose matching edges link to each other (two tops, for example), an edge linked to itself, two children linked both ways on both sides, and a chain whose first child's start links one way to its last child while the last child's end links back to the first child. Debug builds report each of them with a `FlutterError`, as they report a link to an unknown id; baseline links are not followed, so two baselines linked to each other are not reported. Profile and release builds still lay the layout out, including the last kind, which Android never finishes laying out; Android lays out the others as this package does.

## Docs

- [flutter_constraint_layout documentation (Markdown)](https://constraints.birju.dev/docs.md): The entire docs page as one Markdown file. Fetch and read this in full for accurate API usage, constraint syntax, code examples, and layout patterns; prefer it over guessing.
- [Package README (full guide)](https://github.com/BirjuVachhani/flutter_constraint_layout/blob/main/packages/flutter_constraint_layout/README.md): The complete user guide, also shown on pub.dev: every link, dimension, and helper option, z-order, right-to-left rules, sizing and scrolling, the debug overlay, unknown and duplicate ids, common mistakes, Android parity, optimization levels, performance, and the limitations and differences from Android. Read it for anything the docs page does not cover.

## Reference

- [Package on pub.dev](https://pub.dev/packages/flutter_constraint_layout): Versions, API reference, and install instructions.
- [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/BirjuVachhani/flutter_constraint_layout): Repository, issues, and changelog.
- [Live documentation site](https://constraints.birju.dev/docs): The interactive docs, with every example rendered live beside its code.

## Optional

- [flutter_constraint_layout_lints](https://github.com/BirjuVachhani/flutter_constraint_layout/tree/main/packages/flutter_constraint_layout_lints): An analyzer plugin that warns about duplicate and undefined constraint ids (`duplicate_constraint_id`, `undefined_constraint_id`).
- [constraint_engine](https://github.com/BirjuVachhani/flutter_constraint_layout/tree/main/packages/constraint_engine): The pure-Dart layout engine underneath, with no Flutter dependency.
- [Android ConstraintLayout (upstream)](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/views/layout/constraint-layout): The original Android layout this package ports. Its constraint concepts carry over; MotionLayout, `ConstraintSet`, `Layer`, and `Placeholder` are not ported (`Group` is `ConstraintGroup`), and the package README lists the remaining differences.
- [androidx constraintlayout core](https://github.com/androidx/constraintlayout): The Java source the layout engine is ported from.
